title: A Custom GIS System and Workflow Enabling the Targeted Liftout of Cryogenically Frozen Samples for APT and TEM Analysis
content: The nanoscale targeting of interfaces, boundaries, and nanoscale regions is essential for compositional, structural and chemical characterization and analysis using APT and TEM. Such specimen preparation is effectively achieved using Focused Ion Beam-Scanning Electron Microscopy (FIB-SEM) due to its ability to provide both high-resolution imaging and precise material modification or removal. Gas injection system (GIS) gases, such as MeCpPtMe3, W(CO)6,­ or C10H8 are used for precise patterned material deposition of Pt-, W-, or C-based protection layers respectively, the marking of features such as grain boundaries, and the attachment (welding) of lamella to the nanomanipulator probe or substrates. For specimen preparation at room temperature, these traditional GIS gases are reliable. However, at cryogenic temperatures, the thermophysical properties are such that they condense uncontrollably over cryogenically frozen samples which buries the region of interest. Figure 1A and 1B shows a specimen at -190°C before and after exposure to Pt GIS gas (MeCpPtMe3). Although a cryo-based workflow that uses uncontrolled deposition of GIS material [1] or redeposition “nanowelds” [2] for attachment and specimen protection is used throughout the community, this strategy is very challenging and time consuming. Another strategy would be to implement different GIS gas chemistries with thermophysical properties that prevent them from condensing at cryogenic temperatures. The work here describes a GIS delivery platform enabling the experimentation and development of GIS gas chemistries that can be used for precision depositions as in a similar manner as the way traditional GIS gases are used at room temperature. Figure 1C shows a prototype custom nanomanipulator probe compatible with an integrated GIS delivery system allowing the introduction of various GIS gas chemistries without the need to use other chamber ports. As a proof of concept, propane was used as a GIS carbon source to deposit a targeted rectangular pattern on a cryogenically cooled silicon substate without an uncontrolled deposition (Fig. 1D). Figures 1E and F show the targeted welding and lifting of the probe to a particle from the surface. This capability lays a foundation towards performing targeted FIB liftout and specimen preparation in line with a traditionally workflow, but a cryogenic temperature. Other GIS gas chemistries and delivery strategies which do not require a GIS-integrated manipulator probe are also being explored will be discussed.
